We’re rebuilding GitHub’s Git infrastructure while GitHub keeps running, creating a foundation for agent-scale software development.

Share:

Every day on GitHub, millions of developers build the products their customers rely on, contribute to open source, and pursue personal projects. GitHub’s architecture has changed steadily over the years to support that work and the growing demands of the developers and organizations who depend on it.

Agentic software development is driving the next architectural shift. With developers and agents working concurrently in repositories that receive millions of commits a day, these workloads demand a different Git architecture. We’re rebuilding GitHub’s Git infrastructure to support them. This post explores the demands shaping that work and the design principles behind it.

Today’s highest-volume workloads show the scale we’re building for. The gap between a typical repository and the busiest ones is wider than most people expect. Here’s a rough picture of the monthly repository activity distribution on GitHub from August 2026:

Repository activity climbs sharply at the far end of the distribution. The busiest repository on GitHub saw roughly a billion requests in August.

Beyond these highest-volume workloads, total Git activity on GitHub is also growing rapidly: between September 2025 and August 2026, it increased to more than 2x its previous level, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion.

In September alone, developers and agents made 7.38 billion commits on GitHub, more than five times as many as a year earlier.

The repositories at the top of this curve show what agentic development looks like at its leading edge: large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today. We’re investing deeply in Git infrastructure to meet the demands of agentic software development and give teams a foundation built for their most ambitious workloads.

Building for this scale means addressing several architectural challenges:

Commit turnaround becomes a bottleneck per agent. An agent in a tight loop commits or checkpoints after nearly every action. Its speed is bounded by how fast a single push completes, so latency that a human would never notice becomes the limiting factor.

Write throughput demand is increasing by orders of magnitude. Pushes grew 4.9x year over year, from 0.69 billion to 3.35 billion per month. Thousands of agents working on their own branches in one repository produce a sustained write rate that converges on a single point in our architecture.

Merges contend on one reference. Trunk-based development, release trains, and merge queues funnel all that work onto a single ref that has to absorb every merge. Pull request merges on GitHub grew to nearly 4x their volume a year ago.

Each push multiplies into thousands of reads. For example, CI and code scanning clone or fetch the same branch tip thousands of times per minute, and that fan-out has to be cheap. GitHub Actions alone ran 3.26 billion times in September, more than 4x as many as a year ago.

Operations on a repository must continue to be fast. To keep them fast, we continually compact repository data and clean up objects that are no longer needed. Every new write adds to that work, and the cost compounds as volume climbs.

This is why fast clones only solve part of the problem. Reads are relatively easy to scale: add caches, add replicas, and serve the same bytes to more clients. Scaling reads is essential, but these workloads require more than that. Writes are way harder. Every push has to be stored durably and made visible consistently before the next agent or CI job can build on it.

Where today’s architecture meets new demands

The current architecture has served developers well for years. Every repository is stored by Spokes, which keeps a full copy on the local disks of several fileservers, five by default. Those fast local disks let Git operations read native repository data with low latency, and the extra copies provide redundancy while spreading reads across fileservers. When a push updates a reference, a three-phase commit protocol uses a quorum to ensure that CI, the web UI, and API clients see a consistent repository state. That pairing serves a billion repositories today.

However, the mechanism we use for durability is the same one we use for scale. The copies on disk are the source of truth, so adding read capacity means adding another durable replica. Every replica participates in every write, so a push is only as fast as the slowest replica in its set. The net effect: adding replicas to absorb read load makes writes slower.

For most repositories, this tradeoff works well. At the highest activity levels, it becomes a ceiling: adding read replicas adds overhead to writes, losing a replica reduces read capacity, and losing quorum stops writes entirely. To meet agent-first demands, we need to separate durability from scale without losing what teams rely on today.

Built for the busiest, better for everyone

We’re rebuilding the infrastructure while GitHub keeps running. There’s no maintenance window where the world’s code stops moving, and no version of this work where we ask people to change how they build software while we do it.

We’re building for the most demanding workloads on GitHub: an enterprise shipping under strict regulatory requirements, a team landing a change across a repo that builds an operating system, and an organization running thousands of agents against a single codebase. Engineering for that scale raises the floor for everyone. The maintainer reviewing contributions from volunteers across time zones and the student opening their first pull request get the same faster, more resilient foundation.

The new architecture also must preserve the controls teams already operate on. A maintainer needs branch protections and required reviews so an unreviewed change never reaches the default branch. A security team needs audit logs and repository visibility to investigate a suspicious access event. An on-call engineer needs dependable automation and enough observability to understand why a deployment failed.

For the platform to keep serving everyone here while it scales for the busiest workloads, these are our guiding principles:

Build on the workflows developers already trust. Teams rely on workflows like branching, review, merge, and history to build, ship, and govern software at scale. Our new infrastructure is designed to support those same workflows at much higher volumes of activity.

Put reliability first. We measure every decision against the reliability that developers and organizations require. Confidence in the platform is what lets an engineering organization build automation, ship on a schedule, meet compliance obligations, and understand the software it produces. This work will meaningfully improve throughput and scale, and those gains extend a foundation of trust that’s already there.

Keep people in control of their code. If the system isn’t helping the people and organizations who use it, and isn’t under their control, it isn’t worth building. As agents take on more of the work, the people who own the code can still review, understand, and approve it.

The approach

We are building a new GitHub architecture that can scale much more effectively. Our approach centers around core distributed systems design tenets, applied to the concurrency and scale of agentic software development. Our goal is to continue the forward momentum for open-source communities and enterprises around the world who have built their projects with Git and GitHub, while preserving and adapting the features and controls around it to meet the new needs of the agentic era.

Minimize coordination

A repository that receives many pushes must accept and publish updates quickly. Coordination is valuable when it protects correctness, but too much of it limits write throughput and can turn a busy repository into a bottleneck. Our current architecture is tightly coupled in places it doesn’t need to be, which limits our ability to scale across reads and writes without tough trade-offs. We’re redesigning the system to preserve the coordination that Git semantics require and let everything else proceed independently.

Coordinate only what needs agreement. The part of a push that truly needs agreement is the reference update itself. Storing the underlying objects, validating object connectivity, and secret scanning are much more work, but most of it can happen in parallel to other writes. That shrinks the critical path of a push to the small step that needs coordination, so the rest of the work no longer delays the acknowledgment.

Move maintenance off the serving path. Compaction and garbage collection are among the heaviest work a repository does, and today they run on the same hosts that answer live Git requests. In the new architecture, separate workers handle maintenance directly against durable storage. A busy repository can be optimized continuously in the background without slowing pushes and fetches.

Decouple storage from compute

Today, complete repository copies on local disks serve both as durable storage and as the layer that answers Git requests. Separating the two lets us scale each one independently.

Scale reads without adding durable copies. In the new architecture, read capacity comes from lightweight workers that cache data to serve requests. The authoritative copy of the repository lives in a durable storage layer underneath. That way, the platform can absorb large read spikes from CI fan-out, agent fleets, and large clones without adding work to every push.

Let each layer do one job. Authoritative repository data lives in Azure Blob Storage, which already provides durability and replication at Azure scale. The compute layer is optimized for throughput at the lowest latency.

Recover faster from failures. When storage and compute are coupled, losing a host reduces both capacity and durability, and recovery means rebuilding a full repository copy. When they’re separate, losing a compute worker is closer to a cache miss: a replacement worker can start serving requests right away and fill its cache from durable storage as traffic arrives.

Match capacity to demand. Compute workers can be added or removed as traffic changes instead of provisioning for peak load in advance. A repository going through a burst of activity, like a release or a new agent fleet coming online, can get extra capacity for the burst. Once it passes, that capacity goes away.

Together, these tenets allow us to support higher throughput and more concurrent work without abandoning the reliability and controls that our users need.

What comes next

We’re building an architecture designed to provide the highest throughput and reliability available. Reads and writes scale independently, and the system recovers gracefully from failures. In internal benchmarks, it has delivered up to 35 times higher write throughput, with read capacity that scales on its own to meet demand.

As automated development increases the frequency and concurrency of software change, GitHub will evolve its foundations without trading away the governance and control that teams rely on. We’re already putting that foundation in place. In the next post in this series, we’ll dive deeper into our future architecture and the journey that led us there.

We’re launching ReviewBench, a benchmark for code review agents built on representative GitHub pull requests, multi-source ground truth, calibrated evaluation, and production-aligned metrics.

Share:

Agentic code review is becoming an essential piece of how development happens. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships.

But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow.

That makes it important to understand how reviewers actually compare: what different systems catch, what they miss, and the tradeoffs they make. A good code review benchmark should reflect the diversity of real pull requests, capture a broad set of review findings, and support meaningful breakdowns by severity, category, and precision-recall preferences. For teams building code review agents, the benchmark should also provide an offline signal that reliably tracks whether changes are likely to improve the experience in production. Existing benchmarks often make tradeoffs between label quality, coverage, and how well they represent real-world code review, leaving a gap for a rigorous and reproducible evaluation methodology that brings these pieces together.

We built ReviewBench, a new code review offline benchmark, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today. It follows the language, repo size, and size distribution of pull requests, modeled after over 100 million real pull requests on GitHub. It uses a multi-source golden set and a consistent evaluation rubric and has been independently validated by senior engineers. Just as important, with the help of ReviewBench, our offline evaluation of Copilot code review (CCR) has become more effective at anticipating the direction of production experiments, giving us greater confidence that measured improvements reflect meaningful gains for users.

In this post, we’ll walk through how ReviewBench is constructed, how it establishes reliable ground truth and scoring, and how to onboard your own code review system and submit results.

Definitions of terms used in this blog post

Benchmark: A standardized evaluation that tests code reviewers on a common set of pull requests using the same scoring methodology.

Finding: A specific issue surfaced during code review.

Golden set: A validated collection of known findings for each pull request, used as a reference for evaluating what a reviewer catches or misses.

Precision: Of the issues a reviewer surfaces, the proportion that are valid. Higher precision generally means less noise.

Recall: Of the known valid issues, the proportion the reviewer finds. Higher recall means broader coverage.

F1 score: A single score that balances precision and recall equally.

Fβ score: A variation of F1 that lets you put more weight on either precision or recall, depending on your review preference.

How ReviewBench works

Our benchmark is built around five principles:

1. Representative pull requests, not a demo set

We analyzed 103.9 million GitHub pull requests to characterize the real-world distribution of code review workloads. ReviewBench contains 219 pull requests from 187 public open source licensed repositories spanning 19 languages, with its language and repository-size distributions closely matching GitHub overall. The complete benchmark dataset is publicly available.

We make one deliberate adjustment to this distribution: while language and repository size mirror GitHub directly, pull request size is weighted toward the reviewable middle and tail. This reduces the overrepresentation of tiny, single-file changes while preserving more substantive, multi-file pull requests where review quality matters most.

Quick corpus snapshot:

2. Broad ground truth discovery, independently judged

No single reviewer, whether human or model, can identify everything worth finding in a pull request. To build a broader and more reliable golden set for ground truth findings, we follow a three-stage process:

Gather candidate findings from diverse sources. We collect findings from real human reviewers, issues inferred from author follow-up commits, deterministic analysis tools, and multiple frontier LLMs across model families.

Semantically deduplicate overlapping findings. We merge findings that identify the same underlying issue, broadening coverage without allowing agreement across producers to artificially inflate the golden set or making it dependent on any one source’s blind spots.

Validate findings under a shared rubric. The source of a finding does not determine whether it is correct: a finding counts as a true positive only if it is true, relevant, and non-trivial. We use Claude Sonnet 5 as the LLM grader, applying a consistent evaluation rubric across all submissions. For transparency and reproducibility, we publish both the evaluation rubric and the judge used to apply it.

3. Metrics that measure both known and newly discovered issues

Most benchmarks report precision and recall against a fixed golden set. ReviewBench reports six metrics in two families:

Grounded precision, recall, and F1 score use only the existing gold-set labels. They provide the strict, apples-to-apples comparison: of the issues we already know about, how many did the agent find, and what share of its findings matched a known issue?

Augmented precision, recall and F1 score also evaluate findings that do not match anything in the golden set. The judge independently determines whether those unmatched findings are true or false positives, allowing a reviewer to receive credit for valid issues that no producer in the golden set surfaced

That distinction becomes more important as review agents become more capable. A fixed golden set inevitably becomes incomplete as systems discover issues its creators did not anticipate. Augmented metrics let ReviewBench recognize that behavior rather than automatically penalizing it. Because augmented recall expands the denominator based on what each agent discovers, we use grounded recall as the headline cross-system comparison and augmented metrics as an additional per-system diagnostic.

4. Configurable evaluation for different review preferences

There is no single universally optimal review experience. Some developers may want to focus only on critical issues, while others also value lower-severity, non-breaking findings. Some prefer broader coverage, while others prioritize precision and minimal noise. Others may have specialized needs, such as security- or privacy-focused review.

ReviewBench lets results be sliced by severity and category, while precision and recall capture different operating preferences. Users can also adjust β in the Fβ score to place more weight on recall for broader coverage or precision for lower noise. As these preferences change, the leaderboard is re-ranked accordingly, helping users identify the systems that best match their review priorities.

5. Internally audited and reproducibly evaluated

Before release, we asked senior engineers who had not participated in building the benchmark dataset to independently re-label every ground-truth finding from scratch. Their true/false-positive judgments agreed with ReviewBench 96.6% of the time. We version the benchmark dataset, judge, and matcher used in every evaluation, so results can be compared under the same benchmark configuration and revalidated when the benchmark changes. We also publish the validation methodology, agreement measurements, and known threats to validity, so readers can see how benchmark quality is assessed and where uncertainty remains.

Explore ReviewBench

ReviewBench’s research preview version is now available through the ReviewBench website, where you can explore the full benchmark, compare code review agents, and bring your own agent to evaluate and iterate.

With ReviewBench, you can:

Explore the full benchmark dataset. The complete ReviewBench dataset is publicly available, including the pull requests, findings, labels, severity and category annotations. This allows you to inspect exactly what systems are evaluated on and reproduce benchmark results.

Compare systems on the leaderboard. Results from evaluated code review agents using the full benchmark data are published on a common leaderboard, with views across overall performance, severity, category, and different precision–recall preferences.

Bring your own agent and hill-climb. The full benchmark dataset, evaluation methodology, LLM judge prompt, judge model configuration, and self-serve runner are publicly available, so you can evaluate your own code review agent, inspect its strengths and gaps, and iterate against the same benchmark configuration.

How we’ve used ReviewBench

We have used ReviewBench to evaluate Copilot code review (CCR) across successive iterations, giving us a consistent way to measure progress, catch regressions, and prioritize promising changes. Over time, this has helped us improve the product. One of the most valuable benefits of ReviewBench is that it provides an early offline signal of how a change to the product is likely to perform in production. Across experiments evaluated with ReviewBench before A/B testing, offline changes have consistently pointed in the same direction as what we see later in production.

A recent lite-tier experiment provides a concrete example of this broader pattern. We introduced a multi-model ensemble review that combines several independent model runs into a single review rather than relying on a single run. ReviewBench predicted higher precision, recall, and comment volume, along with lower cost per review.

To compare offline and production results, we use corresponding online signals. Addressed rate, our online counterpart to precision, is the percentage of CCR comments that an LLM determines prompted a developer to make a corresponding code change, based on the diff, thread, reactions, resolution state, and post-review code. For recall, we measure how much additional human review is still needed.

The online A/B test moved in the same direction as ReviewBench predicted: addressed rate (precision) rose 8.0%, recall rose 13.6%, and comment volume rose 61%, while cost per review fell 8.0%, all relative to the production control.

Comment volume alone, however, does not capture comment quality. More critical findings mean something very different from low-severity nits. ReviewBench’s severity-level evaluation captured this too: it predicted a 227% increase in critical comments, compared with 262% online, along with the same broader shift toward more moderate comments and fewer nits.

This gives us a fast and repeatable signal before running production experiments. Online experiments remain the ultimate measure of user impact, but ReviewBench gives us greater confidence in which changes are worth taking there.

How to submit your own run

Sign in with GitHub on the ReviewBench website.

Register your agent. Provide a container image, your configuration, and your own model key. We provide the judge.

Try it on the test set. Run against a 25-PR test set with per-PR detail and repeat as you tune your configuration.

Do a final run. When you’re ready, run the full set of 219 pull requests (three rounds), scored by the same judge as every other entry.

Publish to the leaderboard. Your scores remain private until a maintainer reviews and approves the submission. Scores are published to the leaderboard only if they outperform the agent’s current leaderboard score, or if this is the agent’s first leaderboard entry.

We invite you to explore ReviewBench, evaluate your own system, challenge our assumptions, and help us improve the benchmark. We’re excited to collaborate with researchers and practitioners to make code review evaluation more open, reliable, and useful—and ultimately help move AI code review forward.

Acknowledgments

ReviewBench was a team effort across GitHub and Microsoft. We’re grateful to the researchers and engineers who built it: those who designed the methodology, curated the pull requests, built the golden set and the evaluation pipeline, and made the benchmark something anyone can run.

Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.

Share:

Today, one in three pull requests on GitHub involves an AI agent. A year ago, that number was fewer than one in 10. If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human.

If developers and agents move faster, we have a responsibility to ensure protection keeps up with the accelerated rate of code creation. That means preventing more leaks before they happen and making the response to exposures that remain less dependent on manual human effort.

This is a pivotal point for leaked secrets. Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.

In this essay, I share the nine quarters of data behind that claim. I also introduce the fine-tuned classifier we built with Microsoft Applied Sciences to extend push protection to unstructured secrets. The model assesses a whole set of candidate secrets in less than two milliseconds and could more than double the number of secrets that we can prevent.

Outpaced, not careless

A new secret appears in publicly visible code about once every two seconds, doubling yearly for the past three years. Public discourse is quick to jump to the idea that AI made developers careless.

Between Q2 2024 and Q2 2026, screened pushes grew 2.84 times while pushes carrying credentials grew 2.59 times. Across nine complete quarters of data, we found no statistically detectable trend regarding per-push prevalence. At the same time, we found data suggesting that, more than ever, developers understand the risk of accidental exposures and are less willing to accept that risk. Over the same period, the share of push-path blocks overridden by developers fell linearly from 6.63% to 3.93%. These figures challenge the common claim that agents are causing developers to become more careless.

At a fixed rate, doubling activity doubles expected exposures. If each exposure requires the same human response, the workload doubles too. The mean time to manually revoke a secret hovers around 40 days; roughly one in five took more than 90 days. We’re accelerating the creation of software while exposed credentials can remain usable for weeks or months, because human remediation can’t scale at the same pace as development.

Telling developers to be more careful cannot, on its own, solve that problem. As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce human effort required by those that remain, if software development is to remain sustainable.

Prevention scales with compute

I’ve spent the past few years working on secret scanning at GitHub and the past year as product lead for the area. Our greatest impact has come from connecting the dots between detection and systems that can act.

GitHub’s catalog covers more than 150 technical partners through our secret scanning partnership program. Through our partner program, we work with participating secret issuers to build out detectors and report public exposures so they can respond. In Q2 2026, public scanning successfully reported an average of 26 credential matches a second, including repeat observations. Once notified, a large number of these partners immediately revoke the token: OpenAI API keys, Google Cloud account credentials, Slack webhooks, Hugging Face user tokens, SendGrid keys, etc. The owner may still need to replace the token, but revocation can happen without waiting for a developer to find and process a GitHub alert.

Push protection intervenes earlier. It stops recognizable credentials before they enter repository history, giving the developer or agent a chance to correct the change before there’s an exposure to investigate. We work with our technical partners to increase precision rates of their detectors as much as possible, until we’re confident enough to push-protect these secrets for the developer community by default.

Thanks to the efforts of our partners, in the past month, a secret was blocked by push protection at least once every second. When it comes to issuer-bound credentials, GitHub blocks more secrets than those which slip. I’m proud of how ordinary we’ve made that feel for developers.

Remediation scales with people

When including additional secret types, push protection stops about 30% of newly detected secrets before they enter repository history. We find the remaining 70% after the credential is, unfortunately, already lost. And:

Prevention scales with compute, but remediation still scales with people.

Refusing a push costs compute; cleaning up a secret already lost to visible history costs a developer’s time and attention.

As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce the human effort required by those that remain, or else the volume of vulnerabilities introduced will become untenable.

Telling developers to be more careful cannot solve this imbalance. Recognizing more of these secrets, earlier in development flows, is work the platform must take on.

Solving the four-body problem

Before a secret crosses the push boundary, the cost of stopping it is small, and the decision is binary: block or allow. After it crosses, the same string can authenticate to a real system, and the cost is unbounded.

In many cases, our only detection clue may be the surrounding code and world context. A provider-issued token may have a recognizable prefix. An internal database password may be completely unstructured, with no identifying pattern at all. We were already using context to find these secrets post-push; the problem was balancing that context-aware judgement with other factors.

We refer to this as the “four-body problem” for secret protection: precision, latency, throughput, and cost are coupled constraints. Prevention must be worth a developer’s time. A finding suitable for later review may not justify blocking a push. A false positive interrupts a developer and makes the next block harder to trust. A check that is too slow, expensive, or difficult to scale limits how often it can run.

Protection at the push in under 2 ms

Our new ModernBERT classifier assesses candidate secrets in context, without generating code or prose. It’s not only more precise than existing LLM-based pipelines, but it’s incredibly fast, evaluating candidate batches in under two milliseconds. It’s also extremely cost efficient, enough to run at scale in the critical path.

The inclusion of our model in push protection makes it possible for us to more than double the number of secrets that we’re able to prevent. The feature is currently in private preview. Later this month, the feature will be available to organizations with GitHub Secret Protection across Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Teams. It will consume AI credits.

We’re also bringing the model to developer surfaces beyond the push.

Starting today, any organization with AI secret detection will be automatically updated to the new model. Alerts opened from these post-push scans remain included with an organization’s purchase of secret scanning at no additional cost.

The model will also ship with GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23 in public preview, bringing AI-detected alerts to Secret Protection customers even in air-gapped environments.

We’re adding the classifier to the /security-review command for the Copilot CLI and Copilot App, so Copilot users can address secrets before a push even without needing an organization’s GitHub Secret Protection plan. AI credit usage will be attributed to GitHub Secret Protection in your AI usage insights.

Looking forward

The future we want is one where developers can entrust more work to agents without supervising every request, and one where the number of people that an organization needs to keep its credentials safe no longer scales with the amount of code it writes. We owe the developer community the same progress in protecting software that we are delivering in producing it.

We want people to build more software. Our capacity to protect it should grow with our capacity to create it.

Learn how to add custom instructions and skills to your repository, use custom agents, and connect MCP servers like Playwright.

Share:

Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types.

Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task.

In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we’ll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project:

Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow.

Agent skills package repeatable procedures.

Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connect Copilot to external tools and data sources, expanding what it can do.

Let’s look at how each one works and how they can work together.

Start with custom instructions

Suppose you ask Copilot to add a custom page size to an application. Making the change is only part of the job. The new code should also follow the patterns your team already uses.

Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation.

You can also create path-specific instruction files inside .github/instructions. These files use an applyTo field to tell Copilot when the guidance is relevant.

When Copilot works on a matching file, it can use both the repository-wide instructions and the more specific guidance. That lets you keep the broad rules in one place without forcing every file type into the same mold.

Package repeatable procedures as agent skills

Custom instructions are useful for standards that should shape many tasks. But some guidance only matters when Copilot is performing a particular procedure, such as running quality checks, preparing a release, or debugging a failed workflow.

That’s where agent skills come in. A skill is a folder containing instructions and, optionally, scripts and other resources that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Project-level skills can live in .github/skills, with each skill in its own subfolder.

For example, a .github/skills/quality-checks folder could contain a SKILL.md file that explains:

When Copilot should use the skill.

Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting.

What each script checks.

How to troubleshoot common failures.

The description in SKILL.md helps Copilot determine when the skill applies. After updating the interface, Copilot can load the quality-checks skill and follow the project’s established process for testing and linting instead of guessing which commands to run.

Use a custom agent for broader, specialized work

Some tasks are larger than a single procedure. An accessibility review, for example, may require Copilot to inspect components, templates, styles, and interactions across multiple files.

Custom agents let you create specialized versions of Copilot for work like this. A repository-level agent profile lives in .github/agents and can define the agent’s purpose, instructions, tools, and relevant project context.

Use a custom agent when a recurring type of work benefits from a dedicated role or perspective, especially when the task may span multiple files and draw on several tools or sources of context.

Connect Copilot to external tools with MCP servers

Instructions, skills, and agents help Copilot understand how to work within your project. MCP servers expand what it can access and do beyond the repository.

MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, and services. A documentation server can give it access to framework guidance, while a server such as Playwright can let it open and interact with your application in a browser.

You can browse available MCP servers in the Copilot app or add a custom one. Once Playwright is configured, you can ask: Use the Playwright MCP server to test the functionality manually.

Copilot can then use Playwright to open the application in a browser and interact with it much as you would. That gives it a way to verify not only that the code passes automated checks, but also that the updated interface behaves as expected.

Choose the right type of customizations

These customizations solve different problems, but they become more useful when you combine them:

Custom instructions define the conventions Copilot should follow across the repository or for particular files.

Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant.

Custom agents provide focused expertise and guidance for broader tasks.

MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, services, and data sources, expanding what Copilot can do.

Take this with you

Giving Copilot useful project context starts with four questions:

What project convention do I keep explaining?

What multi-step procedure do I repeat?

What complex task could benefit from a dedicated custom agent?

What outside tool or source does Copilot need?

Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made instructions, skills, agents, and more through Awesome Copilot. Find one that addresses a workflow you already repeat, review what it contains, and adapt it to your repository’s tools and standards.

Start small: choose one convention you keep explaining, add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md, and see how Copilot applies it to your next task.

In September, we experienced two incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

Share:

Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months.

The short version of August and September: we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete.

By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added.

We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. We disabled that process during planned handoffs while improving recovery.

Outside the regional migration, 24 authentication-core tables moved off GitHub’s oldest shared database, removing approximately one million queries per second from its replicas. The database cluster supporting issues and pull requests removed approximately 980 million unnecessary edit-history rows, creating an estimated 1.8 terabytes of recoverable storage. Weekly deadlocks fell approximately 77% from their June peak, and continuous cleanup now prevents the same unbounded growth from returning.

Half of sampled pull request traffic can now continue with limited functionality when a shared dependency fails. Production results showed several read operations remained available during a shared-database incident. Database traffic routing can also add capacity automatically during spikes; one group expanded from 14 to 19 instances during a September 23 increase in pull request activity. A production overload control now lets responders protect higher-priority API and web workflows by rejecting lower-priority requests before broader saturation. Operator documentation and training are complete.

GitHub Actions also gained operating headroom. Production changes reduced measured Redis operations by approximately 28% and relative CPU by approximately 30%. A separate infrastructure cache reduced Redis bandwidth by 84%, average response time by 66%, median response time for the primary inventory request by 96%, and queued requests by 95%.

The August 6 actions outage, August 17 github.com outage, September failover disruption, and controlled capacity pause are reminders that measured improvements matter only when they reduce customer risk under real conditions. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

September 13 09:16 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 28 minutes)

What happened?

Impact summary

Duration: approximately 2 hours

Customers may have seen requests fail, run slowly, or remain pending when opening or updating issues and pull requests, calling APIs, creating access tokens, starting GitHub Actions workflows, or signing up.

~96% of the customer requests creating issues through the web interface were impacted during the incident window. In addition, 90% of new customer signup and ~4% of actions workflows also experienced intermittent failures.

What went wrong and why?

A background data-cleanup job increased load on a shared database. The job had a safeguard designed to slow its writes when database replicas fell behind, but the safeguard did not account for incoming load on the primary database server. As a result, the job continued running until the primary reached its connections limit. When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that depended on it could not complete reliably.

Two other factors increased the impact and delayed recovery. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept resending writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover.

How did we respond?

A background data-cleanup job began writing to a shared database.

The job’s safeguard monitored replica lag but did not account for load building on the database’s primary server.

The primary ran out of available connections, causing requests across dependent services to fail or run slowly.

Automated monitoring detected the incident, and we traced the failures to load on the shared database.

We reduced internal load and paused the background job.

The database recovered, and error rates across the affected services returned to normal.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We are implementing additional safeguards to improve database resilience and service availability. These measures will better control background processing based on available database capacity, reduce unnecessary retries during failures, and limit the impact of slow database requests.

We are also improving service startup behavior to ensure that temporary database connectivity issues do not unnecessarily affect service recovery.

September 28 21:16 UTC (lasting 52 minutes)

What happened?

Impact summary

Duration: approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes

This incident impacted Copilot code review across github.com and GHEC data-residency regions. Affected customers saw Copilot remain in a reviewing state without a review appearing, with delays ranging from ~30 minutes to a max of 2 hours.

Some reviews on github.com continued to complete normally during the incident, while reviews in data-residency regions did not. Some customers still received delayed error messages for requests made during the incident.

What went wrong and why?

Copilot code review uses a separate service to run reviews and 2 versions of the results are returned: a limited copy that excludes the review comments and a full copy that includes the completed review. Copilot code review posts reviews only from the full copy. A change to that service began sending the full copy only for some customers. For other customers, only the limited copy was sent.

As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully. The missing review results were not detected due to lack of monitoring. The incident was detected as some of the reviews remained incomplete for more than 30 minutes, triggering an alert to first responders.

We mitigated the incident by reverting the change.

How did we respond?

A change to the service that runs Copilot code reviews began rolling out, and review results stopped appearing on pull requests. The change reached every environment.

Reviews began timing out, triggering an alert to the Copilot code review team. We declared an incident.

We traced the failures to the change and began reverting it.

While the revert completed its required checks, we posted the incident on the GitHub Status page.

The revert then reached all the affected regions. We resolved the incident and advised customers to request affected reviews again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We are strengthening the reliability of Copilot code reviews by adding safeguards throughout the review and delivery process. These improvements will help ensure that completed reviews are delivered successfully, allow failed reviews to recover automatically, and provide earlier notification when issues occur.

We are also improving our monitoring and deployment processes so that problems can be identified and addressed more quickly.

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

There’s been plenty of chatter about AI’s effect on jobs. Will everyone get laid off to train AI? Will every developer become a super generalist? Are there new roles rising from the ashes? But Corey Hymel, head of research at Andela, wanted numbers behind that chatter. He and his team looked at nearly 50,000 job postings to find the skills and roles that are emerging before the industry has properly given them titles. I spoke with him to find out what that research says about the new developer skillsets that land permanent roles.

Q: You did this research on how skills shift and change in job titles. Could you give an intro to this to the project?

A: At Andela, our general approach and methodology to the market is that job titles and resumes are the best worst thing that we have out in the world right now. We're obsessed with understanding very fine-grained skills of what people are able to do.

That's premise number one. Premise number two was that we hear very commonly "Oh, AI is changing jobs. Oh, AI's gonna get rid of jobs," or, "AI is, gonna create new jobs." But it's all very anecdotal and not very data-driven. We looked at it and said, "Is there a way that we can actually go in and put some numbers and some rigor to actually understand what's going on behind the curtains with all of these jobs?" We've got a internal skill taxonomy and ontology that we use that grounds all of this and is the base of the research and data structure that goes in.

But for us, it's really important because the other big side of our business is around learning and upskilling. So how can we provide our customers information around where the industry is heading. Here's some skills that people should be learning that we're seeing become more common. These are the roles. Some of these might fall in between two.

While you might say, "Front-end engineers need to go learn this," actually you probably should pull in product managers as well.I think job titles have always lagged the work, but especially now it's getting worse and worse.

Q: So it's not necessarily about job titles changing, but more about new skills being applied to existing job titles and mid-range roles appearing. I think you talked about DevSecOps as an example of a bleed role.

A: Exactly. What I'm seeing in the news pretty frequently is that this pervasive narrative that AI's gonna make everyone generalist, and it's just turning these jobs into gray jobs where skills can bleed all over.

And what the data shows is that isn't true. There are very niche skill bundles that are either forming as these net new roles that no one's talked about yet or the underlying skills within historical roles are starting to change.

From the labor market or the hiring side, it's, one, happening so quick that people can't keep up with it. Or two enterprises don't really know what skills people should be learning, so they just give up this generalist title of AI engineer. It's like, what what does that mean? There's 100 different flavors of what that could be. But for them it's just easier to say "Oh, we need someone that does AI."

Q: At re:Invent last year, Amazon's CTO, Werner Vogels, talked about the T-shaped developer, where you have a deep focus but a broad base of understanding. Does your data reflect that? Or are you seeing a more specific concentration of these skill bundles?

A: I've gotten that question a few times, and transparently, I've not followed up with it as much as I probably should have. Because you have the T shape and you have the I shape, and I think there's a star shape. I've gotten questions about a few different ones, but from what we're seeing, I think that probably the T shape does typically follow the pattern in the data. But I don't have a definitive answer on that yet.

Q: That's something I'd love to know because, anecdotally, I hear a lot of people talking about this broadening of what a fullstack developer is that's covering product design to SRE. I wonder if people are actually hiring roles for that or if that's just something that happens within organizations.

A: I don't know. We didn't see in the data this idea of a net generalist. But what we are seeing is that if you look at the typical flow of the software development life cycle, if you put roles down in some linear fashion of product manager and then front-end engineer, back end engineer, DevOps, and then QA, the bleed in between those roles are where we're starting to see the most common mix in skills.

So for instance: the front end product engineer. This might be like a like an F-shaped engineer. Meaning that like they lean to one side—they might have a background in front-end engineering, but now they're being asked to stretch into a product role to talk to customers to get feedback, to prioritize and backlog features, and so on.

We're seeing the same thing on the back-end and the DevOps side of back-end engineers now needing to know about deploying these models into production and think about scalability and stuff—that F goes in the other direction.

I need to think about my shapes a little more for this.

Q:That shape is interesting, though. The F shape one— with AI, now that you're able to touch the things that are closest to you, you can branch out, right? Back end engineers can start touching the database and stuff like that.

A: Even to some degree like merging over into prod, even into the front end side too.

Q:What are some of the the skill bundles that you saw in the research?

A: One of the ones our customers often describe but never label was this idea of an LLM application engineer. This is someone that's very versed in building products on top LLMs, whether it's OpenAI APIs or open weight models or Claude code. They know how to plug into the APIs, but they can also take the step beyond that, meaning that they know how to construct the harnesses.

They know and are familiar with things like evals, which when we talk to customers, they think about it as just a backend engineer. That's a very specific skill set. Your classical back-end engineer will not necessarily know about building agent eval harnesses or governance and guardrails. That one was super interesting and also showed up pretty prevalent in the data.

Another one that I've heard it a few times now, is that 2026 and 2027 is gonna be the year of the CFO. How to deal with consumption spending. Now you have new products that are all on these consumption models, which pass-through products. Not only that, but your developers are consuming these new kind of OpEx spends. A FinOps reliability engineer, someone that's able to think about project development and factoring the cost—not just of typical end-user consumption, like cloud consumption—but also developer tooling. When we're building our AI-native SDLC, people talk about financially responsible ways to do this. We hear a lot about how do we optimize our token spend and how do we reduce our token spend. An engineering role that's very keen to understand costs, like in these cases, we use cheaper or faster models with simpler processes, or we design these to have where you might need Fable or something else because it is highly complex,

The last one was this docs-as-code engineer.

We hear a lot about spec-driven development. It’s treated like something that should be pushed down directly on top of developers, when in reality, there is this new role where people that were doing classical technical writing or classical documentation are some of the best spec-driven engineers. They're the ones that construct the context better than developers can to feed into these new models, as well as set the context for long-term agentic development on these bigger code bases.

Q: The AI application engineer is an interesting one—I hear a lot from people that everybody should be building their own software factory. It's interesting to see that these skills are specialized in the data.

A: I think that's the big I think insight with all of this. It challenges the narrative and the status quo of, either one, everyone's just gonna be the expanded fullstack developer, or two, everyone's just a generalist and you can just do everything now. In reality, we are seeing statistically significant trends of specific skill groupings that are coming out in hiring and job data.

Q: Did you notice anything about job titles? Do job titles matter for these skill groupings?

A: In my opinion, job titles are important, especially in this context, because it gives enterprises a way to better describe the work that needs to get done. When you look at an enterprise and how a job gets created, specifically when it comes down to the job title, you've got the individual that's closest to the work. A lot of times they might be someone within the team.

But there's layers on top of it, right? It's gotta go to HR, and then to finance, and then procurement, and then eventually a recruiter. You get this chain of custody, and the work gets more ambiguous as it goes down that chain of custody, not only in the description, but the understanding of what the role should be. What I've seen is that the fallback to a generalist role becomes easier.

I hope that with these more specific job titles, from the person that's closest to the work all the way to the edge recruiter, they're able to accurately describe exactly what needs to get done. A better title for that is really important. Because one, it allows the hiring firm to be more specific, it reduces their time, they get better candidates. It puts them in a better place to succeed.

From the candidate side, imagine I've been a back-end engineer for the past 20 years and I now see a back-end engineering role. I'm just hitting apply because I just need to get a job, right? The odds of me ending up in a position where I won’t be successful is relatively high because the underlying skills and requirements and understanding could be vastly different.

I do think in this case it is it is important for these new titles to come along.

Q: In the research post you talked about talent debt. What is talent debt?

A: Talent debt accrues the same way that technical debt does. But the difference with talent debt is that the skill half-life is shrinking substantially. Back in the day, you could go and get a job as a Java engineer and work for 20 years doing Java programming and be okay. But now what we're seeing is that the pace of change is going so fast that the half-life of how long those skills stay relevant is shrinking substantially.

What you get is this skill compression, which then forms into talent debt. A lot of companies are experiencing it now where all of a sudden this race into AI, they look at what they have on the bench and say, "Oh my goodness, we've got nothing even close to what we have to do here."

They have two options then. One is either try to reskill who you have already. Upsides are that you get to keep the strong domain knowledge of the individuals within your team, understand strong system knowledge, and it's good to invest in your people.

The flip side is to try to hire it out. It's faster, but you don't have the domain knowledge, you have ramp time, and you have the the risk of putting the wrong butt in the wrong seat. All of that compounds into this concept of talent debt, which is very similar to technical debt.

Q: Developers have always had to keep learning on the job, right? Even if you're a Java engineer for 20 years, you're learning new frameworks, new features come out, new libraries. Is this acceleration a different sort of thing, where it's not just learning new things for Java, but learning a whole new thing every six months?

A: I think so. It's one thing to pick up a new framework, right? It's one thing to pick up a new programming language. I think a lot of developers are fine with that. The big difference now is that it's a fundamental bedrock shift of the way that you actually work.

That is the big, hard transition. Changing from procedural to object-oriented programming makes you really think structurally about how these things get built, what are ways to optimize and go faster. For a lot of people, that's a stiff change. If you've ever tried to switch between the two, doing C or something procedural into an object-oriented framework, you conceptually think about things much differently.

It's thinking conceptually differently, but at a much bigger scale of how you work as a person. For an engineer, it's going beyond and having to relearn syntax or language or frameworks or methodologies, but into a structural re-understanding how you put all of these new tools to work. How do I actually step back from the code, and how do I adjust in my mind what accountability is and give that to a virtual synthetic knowledge worker.

The engineers that are able to move in between it are ones that have substantial advantage. There’s an engineer working with me from our network making some updates to one of our platforms. He gave me a quote on the time because it was adding some leaderboards in, and I said, "We just need to add a leaderboard. You go give it to Claude Code. This should be an hour."

He was looking at it over four days, so I asked him, "Why does it take so long? Like coding tools are you using?" He uses Claude Code to understand it, but still hand codes everything to a large degree. He doesn't practice agentic development, mostly because he feels accountable for the code that he ships. “If something that I ship is wrong, then that's on me."

I have another developer that just gives it to Claude. If it works, if it passes the unit test and the acceptance test and the smoke test, then ship it to prod. Who cares.

It's interesting to see these different dynamics, but the other underlying one was that the developer that was very hesitant about using it has been using the tools for a while, but has a very small token budget. I think that there's like this fluency gap between those that can, developers that can afford to like fully embrace this new world and have the budget to burn the tokens to get the comfortability with it versus a large group of people that don't. That might be another area of study.

Q: You’re talking about scaling up and becoming comfortable with the tools, but I've heard a lot about AI affecting developer skills, de-skilling, growing lazier with cognitive offloading, people knowing less about the code., Like you said with the the one that's in YOLO mode—if it works, who cares how it works? Do you think AI will make the rescaling and the scaling up harder or easier?

A: I believe there's a lot of different answers to it. On one degree, AI will make upskilling a lot easier, right? You have a personalized tutor. It can explain things to you. I've seen good engineers ask Claude to quiz them on the code so that they get a firm understanding.

Is there gonna be skill degradation? For sure. I think that's one of the premises of any new technology that comes out. Gartner had this skill atrophy onion where you have your core skills that make you who you are. You've got skills that are unique to your domain that are not usually replaceable. Then you have this middle onion skill, which are these skills that are okay to atrophy. For a developer, that might be things like understanding the syntax. I don't necessarily need to know Go to write a Go program anymore. Is that an okay thing to let go? There are some skills in there, maybe general architectural setup that still trigger the sniff test of this doesn't seem just right.

Engineers that have been around for a while that are okay with letting some of these skills go and gaining these new ones are gonna be in extremely good position to accelerate forward. The people that I have concern about are individuals coming into the market now that haven't had time to develop that innate sniff test of when things are going awry and just blindly YOLO stuff. Upskilling and reskilling and skill atrophy or degradation is gonna be a problem in five, ten years when that gap forms.

Or maybe who cares? We weren't allowed to use calculators in school. Now everyone's got calculators, and we turned out fine.

Q: Nobody's coding in Assembly anymore, right? Doesn't matter.

A: Exactly.

Q: For folks who are a little antsy about the future of their jobs and their skills, does this data validate those fears?

A: I think there is a lot of noise about AI making everyone general. There is a lot of AI noise around AI changing jobs. But what we found is that there are new specific skill sets coming out becoming extremely important. People should understand where they fit. We've got another tool where you can put in your current role and we can show you the new role that it's morphing into.
